episodes.158173: A mix of wet and dry thunderstorms produced multiple outflows, that led to one instance of a severe wind gust.
episodes.158265: Severe thunderstorm wind gusts measuring 67 mph were measured by a Wyoming Department of Transportation sensor along United States Highway 20 at Van Tassell on the evening of the 24th.
episodes.158269: Gusty winds developed behind weakening thunderstorms during the evening hours over the bay of Green Bay and Lake Michigan waters.
episodes.158403: Strong instability developed ahead of a dryline under cyclonic flow aloft which produced isolated severe thunderstorms on the afternoon of the 25th. Hot and dry conditions became favorable for these storms to support strong downdrafts that produced severe wind gusts. Later in the evening, additional scattered thunderstorms developed in the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle and tracked eastward. This second round of thunderstorms also generated severe wind gusts through early in the morning of the 26th.
episodes.158463: A line of strong thunderstorms and heavy rain moved through Iowa on the 24th, which led to flash flooding for some areas. The areas seeing the largest impact were in Jefferson and Van Buren Counties in Iowa. The environment in which these storms were in not only favored thunderstorms, but heavy rain, as moisture indices were near record level. Very efficient rain rates were seen, where 2 to 3 inches per hour were common.
episodes.158548: Training storms developed across southeast Nebraska, produced strong winds and caused flash flooding.
episodes.158733: An upper-level disturbance interacting with a slowly approaching warm front triggered clusters of showers and thunderstorms across central Illinois during the evening of June 24th into the early morning hours of June 25th.  Widespread rainfall of 1 and a half to 2 and a half inches occurred...with isolated amounts in excess of 3 inches.  One of the thunderstorm cells produced wind gusts of around 60mph, which caused minor damage in the town of Lowder in Sangamon County.
episodes.158734: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed along an old outflow boundary along the I-72 corridor during the late afternoon and evening of June 25th.  Five brief tornadoes touched down, resulting in minor tree and crop damage.
episodes.158796: A mid-level inverted trough associated with an upper level low pushed across the region and worked in concert to sufficient moisture to develop scattered showers and thunderstorms across the Biscayne Bay waters. A few of these storms produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.158863: Surface observations showed a fairly sharp trough of low pressure located just east of Flagler Beach which arched northeast over the local coastal waters. This trough shifted westward through the day and allowed a plume of deeper moisture to overspread the local area. This surge of moisture under steeper lapse rates and cooler 500 mb temp near -10.8 C under weak shear (< 20 kts) fueled storms with locally heavy rainfall.
episodes.159064: Isolated to scattered strong-to-severe thunderstorms rumbled across various parts of South Central Nebraska on this Friday afternoon and evening, although the majority of activity focused north of Interstate 80. Between 3-8 p.m. CDT, six separate storms (five north of I-80) received Severe Thunderstorm Warnings based on radar indications of at least marginally-severe hail/winds. However, ground-truth reports were tough to come by, with the only two verifying reports consisting of: 1) quarter size hail near Hazard in far southern Sherman County...2) estimated 60 MPH winds and some downed tree limbs in the town of Polk. Based on radar signatures, other portions of counties most favored to have also experienced severe-criteria hail and/or wind included: southeastern Sherman, northern Greeley, southern Kearney and east-central Merrick. Storm mode was a mix of isolated supercells and multicell clusters. The most prominent supercells (albeit fairly small in areal extent) consisted of one that tracked from extreme northeast Dawson County to along the Sherman/Buffalo County line between 3-5 p.m. CDT, and another that initiated along the Phelps/Kearney County line around 6:30 p.m. CDT and drifted southeastward through Kearney County for about an hour before weakening (this was the only local severe storm south of I-80). Timing-wise, although all severe-warned storms within South Central Nebraska occurred between 3-8 p.m. CDT, at least spotty weak activity developed as early as 1-2 p.m. CDT (mainly in far western counties) and weak convection lingered as late as 10-11 p.m. CDT in far southeast counties before departing/dissipating for the night. ||In the mid-upper levels, this event was forced by a combination of larger-scale lift out ahead of a positively tilted trough axis centered from North Dakota into the Central Rockies by early evening, along with more localized lift from a mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) wandering through western Nebraska. The seasonably-early initiation of afternoon convection was also aided by relatively cool mid-level temperatures (only around 8C at 700 millibars). At the surface there were no prominent features in the light wind regime across South Central Nebraska at mid-afternoon, although a subtle west-southwest to east-northeast oriented front bisected the area (possibly a remnant outflow boundary from early-morning Kansas convection), with dewpoints averaging mid-upper 60s (F) on either side of it. Although mixed layer CAPE only peaked around 1500 J/kg, decent effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots clearly promoted severe storm development, including the few supercells.
episodes.159369: Thunderstorms increased in coverage and intensity during the evening hours as more organized activity moved east out of New Mexico and developed into a broken line from I-40 near Endee, NM northeast to around Texline, OK. The northern portion of the line encountered a more favorable environment for strong to severe storms with potential for rotation from near Palo Duro Reservoir to Perryton. Large hail was reported north of Perryton up to the size of ping pong balls which combined with strong winds took out some windows on a farmhouse along with other damage around the property. As this storm moved northeast it created winds estimated 85-90 mph since it took out several power distribution poles from Balko to Elmwood, OK leaving much of Beaver County without power. This storm quickly weakened not long after causing the power loss.
episodes.159370: Thunderstorms increased in coverage and intensity during the evening hours as more organized activity moved east out of New Mexico and developed into a broken line from I-40 near Endee, NM northeast to around Texline, OK. The northern portion of the line encountered a more favorable environment for strong to severe storms with potential for rotation from near Palo Duro Reservoir to Perryton. Large hail was reported north of Perryton up to the size of ping pong balls which combined with strong winds took out some windows on a farmhouse along with other damage around the property. As this storm moved northeast it created winds estimated 85-90 mph since it took out several power distribution poles from Balko to Elmwood, OK leaving much of Beaver County without power. This storm quickly weakened not long after causing the power loss.
episodes.159371: Thunderstorms formed along an old outflow boundary associated with previous day's activity from Endee, NM to Amarillo, TX and along Highway 60 to Canadian, TX. Additional thunderstorms formed in SE CO and eventually traveled along the northern edge of the OK Panhandle from west to east as an upper level trough and cold front approached. The environment was primed for damaging winds and large hail given marginal wind shear but high instability in the area. Automated weather equipment located throughout both the OK and TX Panhandle measured wind gusts from these storms well over 60 mph. The highest wind gust measured was 85 mph at the mesonet located near Hooker, Oklahoma. Some thunderstorms wind damage was also reported especially in Texas County, Oklahoma. The largest hail stone reported was 1.5 inches in diameter near Lipscomb, TX. One of the thunderstorms produced a brief tornado that took out a barn with an RV inside near McLean, TX.
episodes.159372: Thunderstorms formed along an old outflow boundary associated with previous day's activity from Endee, NM to Amarillo, TX and along Highway 60 to Canadian, TX. Additional thunderstorms formed in SE CO and eventually traveled along the northern edge of the OK Panhandle from west to east as an upper level trough and cold front approached. The environment was primed for damaging winds and large hail given marginal wind shear but high instability in the area. Automated weather equipment located throughout both the OK and TX Panhandle measured wind gusts from these storms well over 60 mph. The highest wind gust measured was 85 mph at the mesonet located near Hooker, Oklahoma. Some thunderstorms wind damage was also reported especially in Texas County, Oklahoma. The largest hail stone reported was 1.5 inches in diameter near Lipscomb, TX. One of the thunderstorms produced a brief EF1 tornado that took out a barn with an RV inside near McLean, TX.
episodes.159463: Deep Gulf moisture fed into the state with the LLJ pushing a warm front north into southern Iowa through the late evening. Storms motion was generally parallel to the boundary, resulting in training of storms across southern Iowa and heavy rain. Many locations in southern Iowa received 3 to 6 inches of rain in a few hours with one location reporting over 7 inches of rain.
episodes.159486: An upper level ridge was centered over north central Texas. There was high moisture across West Texas. A surface trough had developed across the Guadalupe Mountains and mountains of West Texas. Fairly hot temperatures were in place across the area. These conditions resulted in a thunderstorm that developed in Loving County that produced wind damage.
episodes.159500: Heavy rainfall associated with a thunderstorm in the Cameron Peak burn area, produced flash flooding in Masonville.  Heavy rainfall, up to one inch in an hour, produced flash flooding along Buckhorn Road, south of Big Bear Road.  Running water, up to 6 inches deep, covered the roadway.  Heavy rain also produced minor flooding in the East Troublesome burn area.  Runoff from that storm impacted a small section of Trail Ridge Road along Onahu Creek. A swath of black water, approximately 100 yards wide and 5 inches deep, inundated the roadway briefly and lasted only about 5 minutes. Trail Ridge Road was closed temporarily to clear away the mud.  There were some minor mud and flooding issues on Green Mountain Trail too.  Finally, a severe thunderstorm produced hail up to quarter size in southwest Boulder.
episodes.159511: A broad upper level ridge was over the Southern Plains. There was a slight moisture gradient in place from the Upper Trans Pecos down to the Big Bend. Temperatures across West Texas were hot, and there was fairly high instability across the area of higher moisture. Wind shear was marginal with the highest shear values in the Permian Basin. These conditions resulted in thunderstorms that produced strong winds and wind damage across portions of West Texas.
episodes.159535: An extremely moist airmass was in place as storms erupted along a stationary front during the afternoon hours. Due to the high moisture content of the airmass, the storms were very efficient rainfall producers with some producing 3 to 4 inches of rain per hour. Marion County saw the most impactful flooding with numerous evacuations and water rescues taking place across the county. Southeast Kansas also saw serious flooding with the Neosho River seeing significant rises.||These same storms also produced pockets of severe downburst winds with the town of Newton taking the brunt of the wind damage. These same storms resulted in an injury when straight-line winds severely damaged a mobile home in southeast Reno County.
episodes.159570: On the evening of June 24th, thunderstorms developed in east-central Colorado due to a lee-side trough in the region. These thunderstorms produced hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts up to 80 mph in the area.
episodes.159572: On the evening of June 24th, thunderstorms developed in northwestern Kansas due to a lee-side trough in the region. These thunderstorms produced hail up to half-dollar size and damaging wind gusts up to 86 mph in the area. The wind gusts had caused a live tree limb that was several feet long to snap off a tree.
episodes.159577: Flash flooding occurred in far northeastern Kansas, and damaging wind occurred across the area due to multiple rounds of rain late in the evening on 6/24 through the overnight hours.
episodes.159578: Scattered thunderstorms created severe weather across central and east-central during the afternoon and evening hours on 6/25.
episodes.159638: On June 25th video of debris flow running over north bound interstate 15 just north of the Utah border in Oneida county was seen.    Radar estimated 2 inches of rainfall in that area resulting in the debris flow and flooding.
episodes.159648: Thunderstorms moved into western Oklahoma from the Texas panhandle during the late evening of the 25th, with several reports of severe wind gusts.
episodes.159746: An area of storms moved across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon and evening of June 24th. These storms produced some minor roof damage to a barn southeast of Riplinger (Clark County). A few trees were blown down near West Salem (La Crosse County). Some of these storms also dropped hail and the largest reported hail was half dollar sized near Willard (Clark County).
episodes.159957: Thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a stationary front over the eastern Sandhills during the early evening hours of June 25th. This activity became severe over Garfield and Wheeler counties with wind gusts estimated at 60 MPH.
episodes.160069: Late in the afternoon, and through the evening hours on June 24 a cluster of storms over southeast Nebraska congealed into a line of thunderstorms that focused across northern Missouri. Most notably within this line of storms was a cluster of QLCS tornadoes that formed in Grundy County. There may have been other tornadoes associated with circulations that were noted on radar, but emergency management confirmed damage consistent with tornadoes near Trenton and Laredo Missouri. Most of the damage was minor, but some grain bins being blown off their foundation was the highlight of the damage in the area. Rainfall was the other big story with this event as some areas received 6 to 10 inches of rain. Despite the excessive rain, the flash flooding was rather minor, however there were still numerous roads closed, and areas near Excelsior Springs were especially hard hit as the Fishing River rose out of its banks. Another semi-dramatic event occurred along I-29 just north of St. Joseph, where a crane that was being used to do road construction became unbalanced and tipped.
episodes.160080: An embedded mid level disturbance helped to develop showers and storms across the region through the early evening on this day, with strong to severe storms occurring across El Paso County through the far southeast plains. In this location high instability and strong forcing provided a setup for large hail and damaging winds to occur. The largest hail of 4 inches occurred across Kiowa county.
episodes.160081: An upper level system moved across the region with scattered storms lifting out across the far southeast plains through the afternoon and evening. Severe storms were possible on this day with one developing across Baca county, producing large hail.
episodes.160170: The remnants of a mesoscale convective system became the focus for thunderstorm development over Lake Pontchartrain and the Mississippi Sound. As this feature drifted northward with weak onshore flow, a line of persistent thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall which led to flash flooding over St. Tammany Parish.
episodes.160194: On the afternoon of June 25th, thunderstorms developed in southwestern Nebraska ahead of an approaching cold front. These thunderstorms produced damaging hail up to half dollar in size within the area.
episodes.160195: On the afternoon of June 25th, thunderstorms developed in east-central Colorado ahead of an approaching cold front. These thunderstorms produced a wind gust of 65 mph in the area.
episodes.160197: On the evening of June 25th, thunderstorms developed in northwestern Kansas ahead of an approaching cold front. These thunderstorms produced wind gusts up to 67 mph in the area and damaging hail up to golf ball size in the area.
episodes.160282: A stalled out surface low across the area lead to a week of conditions favorable for funnel cloud development. In the afternoon and evening hours of June 25, 26, 27, 29, and 30, funnel clouds were reported across Iowa. 0-3 km CAPE values around 100 J/kg and surface vorticity in the vicinity of the surface low made for a good funnel cloud environment for several days, though there was no report of any tornadic activity with any showers.
episodes.160333: A surge in moisture associated with the leading edge of a tropical wave combined with daytime heating and local effects to generate shower and thunderstorm activity during the early to mid-afternoon hours.
episodes.160451: A fair weather waterspout was observed over the open water.
episodes.160465: Late in the afternoon, and through the evening hours on June 24 a cluster of storms over southeast Nebraska congealed into a line of thunderstorms that then pushed southeast into northeast Kansas with isolated severe weather consisting of 1 inch hail and isolated wind damage. Rainfall was the other big story with this event as some areas received 6 to 10 inches of rain. Despite the excessive rain, the flash flooding was rather minor.

episodes.160569: A trough moved southeast through the region, generating a complex of showers and storms.  Numerous reports of damaging winds, a few tornadoes and flash flooding were reported with this system.
episodes.160570: A trough moved southeast through the region, generating a complex of showers and storms.  Numerous reports of damaging winds, a few tornadoes and flash flooding were reported with this system.
episodes.160608: A frontal boundary from the day before sagged further south across south central Kansas with isolated storms developed along it. With ample shear and instability, storms became supercellular with hail the main threat. Later in the evening storms pushed out of Colorado and northwestern Kansas with damaging winds the main threat with good DCAPE values and setting sun.
episodes.160665: A composite outflow boundary extending from the Kansas City area towards southeast Missouri was a focus for new development from the evening hours of June 25th through June 26th. There were numerous reports of damaging winds and flash flooding with this event, as well as a tornado.
episodes.161879: Scattered thunderstorms in late June produced isolated damaging winds and flash flooding.

A brief tornado touched down to the northeast of Renseselaer very early in the morning on June 25th. The tornado first touched down along County Road 429. The tornado quickly pushed northeast, doing damage to a few sheds at the intersection of County Road 429 and Highway MM. One shed was completely destroyed and its roof was lifted into a nearby tree. The tornado spread northeast across Highway MM, before lifting just to the north of Highway MM. The tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 0.21 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. No injuries or deaths were reported.

A brief, narrow tornado touched down in a residential subdivision northwest of Hannibal, MO early Friday morning. The tornado first touched down along Rosewood Drive, where it ripped the siding off the westward facing wall of a residential home. The tornado then continued northeast towards Deer Ridge, completely destroying a couple of vinyl fences and breaking limbs off a large tree on the north side of Deer Ridge. The tornado quickly lifted as it pushed east towards Munger Lane. The tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 0.13 miles and a max path width of 25 yards. No injuries or deaths were reported.

Widespread flash flooding was reported across the southern half of Boone County, when up to 7 inches of rain fell in a span of 6 hours. Several water rescues were reported, including one swift water rescue.  Columbia firefighters rescued a man who was clinging to a tree in Bear Creek downstream of North Creasy Springs Road after his car got swept away by the swift current.  They also rescued two people from a mobile home on North Hinkson Creek Road.  At least an additional 10 water rescues were performed after the drivers drove into flood waters in a number of locations around the county. Numerous roads were flooded including U.S. Highway 63 at intersection with Highway 163, Nifong Boulevard at Glen Eagle Drive, Highway WW at Old Hawthorne, Creasy Springs and Bear Creek, North Route V at Barnes School Road, and U.S. Highway 40 near Midway.  The rain pushed Hinkson Creek to a record high level, flooding Wilson���s Total Fitness and the Missouri Athletic Center at Forum Boulevard and closing Providence Road through midday on Friday.  A section of West Dripping Springs Road was washed out due to flash flooding from Silver Fork Creek.  Highway E was flooded where it crosses over Perche Creek and Route ZZ was flooded by Harmony Creek. Also, Route Y east of Ashland was closed due to flooding from Cedar Creek.  No deaths or injuries were reported.

Another round of heavy rain fell across Boone County, less than 12 hours after the flash flood event from June 24th through the morning hours of June 25th, where up to 7 inches of rain fell. Up to an additional 2 to 3 inches fell causing another round of flash flooding across the county. Numerous roads were flooded.  One water rescue due to swift water took place about 3 miles northeast of Murry. Another swift water rescue occurred about 2 miles northeast of Easley where two occupants of a vehicle were trapped by the flood waters.  Two vehicles were stuck in swift water from Rocky Fork Creek on North Creekland Drive, just north of intersection with East Calvert Hill Road, so the occupants had to be rescued.  Three miles northeast of McBaine, water was flooding a residence, so fire fighters had to rescue the two occupants and their dog.  A section of road was washed out about 5 miles east southeast of Harrisburg.  No injuries were reported.
